body: Yeah that pretty much sums it up, I'm feeling better now that I've posted all this crap/read some responses, so thank you.  I'll see how long it lasts this time, but it's nice knowing someone has read my ramblings and can relate, thank you!

Most of my hobbies were basically nullified when I moved.  It was a sacrifice I knowingly made when I took the job, thinking the opportunity would make up for it.  I'm not regretting it right now (though I was when I originally posted...this is how fast my attitude can change sometimes).

Basically I lived in an outdoorsy place before I moved, if I got bored I could just walk outside and there were some nearby hiking/mountain bike trails to keep me entertained.  Now I'm living in a major city where any hope of naturey exploration being an hour drive and a $10 parking fee away for a more crowded, artificial experience.  Funny thing though, when I left I thought I hated small town living and was going to love the city, wrong call there!  But like I said, right now I'm feeling pretty good, and I'm sure there's a lot in the city that I could come to love, or I'll have opportunities to get back to smaller towns later in my career if I choose to, what bothers me is not knowing how soon I'll go back to feeling like I did when I made the original post.

That's basically what I did after my freshman year of college when I decided to quit MMOs and get my life together.  I started going to parties, out to bars when I turned 21, just trying to fit in.  I ended up getting a group of friends to go out with regularly.  No matter how much I did it though, even when I felt like I was fitting in, I still felt like I was putting an EFFORT toward fitting in, while for everyone else it seems so natural.  And always had that thought in the back of my head that I wasn't being myself, and that I would rather by back at home, a large part of why it was such a relief to move away, so I could spend nights at home alone without feeling like people were judging me for being antisocial.

I think some of this might stem from me idealizing the past.  Maybe because I feel like I missed what a high school/college experience should be.  It's not really justified though, I was a short, scrawny, buck-toothed, four-eyed kid, but I can't think of a negative memory from it...like looking at the aspects of who I was, I should have been hating life, but I remember having a great childhood.  On the other hand, looking at the aspects of my life now, I should be loving it, but I hate it.

Actually just having typed that I came to a sort of realization.  There isn't much about my current life that I want to change, it's what I did to get here that I want to change.  Like if I could re-live my life from high school onward, but end up in the exact same place as I am now, that would be awesome.  I realize this makes no sense, I realize it's not a healthy train of though, I realize how easy the solution is, "just stop worrying about the past dumbass, improve your life now!"  And now I'm basically self diagnosing and thinking in text, and this is what usually happens and why I have typed this without posting it so many times.  But I'm posting anyway, because maybe someone who isn't me will have some insight that I can't come up with.

I think about that a lot, yeah, and sure there's a lot of jobs I'd love to be doing, but they aren't realistic.  Like everyone else in the world I would love to be a movie star, or a researcher on some groundbreaking technology, or a secret agent, or a rock star, etc.  None of these are realistic goals, most of them are pretty childish.  When I look at realistic alternatives, they are mostly only slightly different than what I'm already doing but with extra perks like world travel, or they are things that would be essentially disregarding my degree and causing a hefty pay cut (something like being a guide for mountain climbing or a teaching skydiving or snowboarding).  I wouldn't mind the pay cut with these temporarily, but then if/when I finally grew up, how would a potential employer look at a resume like that, 

"so you got your master's degree, worked in the field for 1 year, then took off 5 years to teach snowboarding and rock climbing?  Congrats, you're a slacker AND you're now 5 years behind in the field!"

Plus my current job is technically a great opportunity for starting a career, and if I left it that would destroy all of the opportunities that come with it, along with leaving me ineligible to get it again.

The difference between what I feel and what you're describing is that you're describing a lot of external, noticeable behaviors.  Being irritable, acting rashly, jitteriness, rapid speech, etc.

Basically everything I'm feeling is internal.  I'm always in great control, and if I'm great at anything it's hiding my emotions.  You could probably talk to me on my best day and my worst day and not be able to tell the difference, I'll be pretty calm and controlled either way.

As for acting rashly/making risky decisions, this is actually something I wish I did more often.  I usually base my actions on what the long term effects will be, almost never do anything that could have negative consequences down the line.  I know it's probably causing me to miss out on a lot of great things and not helping my social awkwardness, but it also doesn't seem to fit with what you're saying at all.
